sections.h2: Paying your Ohio County tax bill
sections.html:
Walk-in payments are accepted at the sheriff's tax office, 301 South Main Street, Hartford. If you would rather mail a check, address it to PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347. The phone line is 270-298-4444.

The counter opens at 8 a.m. and closes at 4 p.m. Monday through Friday. On the first and last Saturday of every month it is open until noon. A drop box hangs on the door for evenings and weekends. Mailed checks are honored by postmark, but never mail cash. A card works at the counter, and the sheriff's website has an online payment link. Refunds, for instance after an assessment is corrected, are mailed once a month near the end of the month, and refund questions go to the same phone line.

Values are not the sheriff's job. Questions about an assessment, the address on a bill or an exemption belong with the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA), 270-298-4433.

sections.h2: What Ohio County looks like for a seller
sections.html:
Land stretches a long way in Ohio County and people are spread thin. Hartford is the seat, Beaver Dam is the biggest town, prices are modest and almost nothing new gets built, so listings are nearly all resales. Population is 23,934 for July 2025, up 0.7 percent from April 2020.

  • A typical owned house is worth $121,400, and owners with a mortgage spend $1,105 a month on housing.
  • Of the 9,107 households, 77.2 percent own.
  • Household income is $57,798 at the midpoint.
  • The county has 10,377 housing units and issued just 3 building permits in 2025.
  • Rent at the midpoint is $739 monthly.

With so little turnover, pricing can be hard. A house in Fordsville, Rockport or McHenry often has fewer nearby sales to compare against than one in Beaver Dam, so lean on recent closed sales and a good photo record of repairs.

Bills become payable on October 1, and the assessment date behind every bill is January 1. This is the calendar the sheriff follows.

Ohio County collection calendar
DatesAmount due
October 1 to November 1Bill less 2 percent
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to 31Face amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Face amount plus 21 percent
After April 15Bill transfers to the County Clerk

State law, in KRS 134.015, names a 10 percent charge for the late period, so ask the tax office to price your parcel exactly before you send a check.

Still no bill around October 10? Phone the tax office and ask for a duplicate, which can come by mail, fax or email. Sending one to a different address is a favor, not a change of record. Only the PVA updates the mailing address on file.

sections.h2: What happens to bills left unpaid on April 15?
sections.html:
Prior-year payments leave the sheriff on April 15 and go to the Ohio County Clerk at 301 S Main St, Suite 201 in Hartford (weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; recording desk 270-298-4423). The clerk's delinquent tax page lists the sale date, so call for the next one.

  • The bill becomes a recorded lien, and 1 percent interest is added each month.
  • Large-scale bidders (over three certificates here, five statewide or $10,000 in total) register with the state first.
  • A listed house with a certificate needs a written payoff from the clerk, since the balance grows each month.

Clearing the balance early is cheaper. After an investor buys the certificate, the debt is owed to that investor with extra fees on top.

Your first call goes to the PVA, 270-298-4433, and the required conference must take place while spring inspection is still open. Bring comparable sales, repair estimates and photos. If the conference fails, the next stops are a form at the County Clerk, then a local three-person board, then the state Board of Tax Appeals. The PVA appeal guide spells out each deadline, including 30 days to reach the state board.

Do not hold back payment during an appeal. If the value drops, the difference comes back as a refund.

sections.h2: A year in the life of an Ohio County bill
sections.html:
Here is the full cycle. Value and ownership are fixed as of January 1. Bills become payable October 1, and the discount window shuts November 1. The face amount holds until the end of December, then penalties begin in January and step up in February. By April 15 anything still owed has left the sheriff's hands.

For a seller, that rhythm decides who pays what. A spring seller still owes the year's bill, since the house was theirs on January 1, and normally gets repaid by the buyer for the later months. A fall seller should check whether the 2 percent discount applies before the bill goes out the door. Whichever season you sell in, bring the most recent receipt to the closing agent along with the sheriff's phone number.

Residents who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, can claim the homestead exemption. A 70 percent VA rating or a 100 percent Social Security disability finding can also qualify, and the PVA decides each claim. It takes a set dollar amount off the assessed value, revised on a two-year cycle, and the next owner starts a new application.

Working farmland is taxed on what the land earns from farming, not on market price. In a county where 76 percent of residents live in rural areas, that can matter a great deal, so ask the PVA about any tract you plan to sell or split.

sections.h2: What a seller owes besides the tax bill
sections.html:
Kentucky's transfer tax lands on the seller. KRS 142.050 sets it at 50 cents for each $500 of declared value, rounding up, and the clerk wants it paid before the deed is accepted.

  • Ask the sheriff whether this year's bill is paid and by whom.
  • Check with the clerk for liens or certificates on record.
  • List a mailing address for future tax bills in the deed, which KRS 382.135 requires.

Any closing after January 1 leaves that year's bill in your name, so divide it in the contract and save the receipt.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has tax problems
sections.html:
You can sell with taxes unpaid. The title company subtracts what is owed from your proceeds. Before April 15 the sheriff gives you the figure, and after it the County Clerk does. Work through it in this order.

  1. Ask the right office for a written payoff that stays valid through closing.
  2. Pass the number to the title company.
  3. Make sure the clerk shows any lien as released.
  4. File the receipts.

Selling for cash avoids a lender's appraisal and repair demands, which suits an older house. The tax payoff still gets made at closing. Self-employed owners and heirs with a vacant property should also check that nothing is recorded against the parcel before choosing a closing date.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Ohio County property tax?
faqs.a: At the sheriff's tax office, 301 South Main Street in Hartford, or by check to PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347.

faqs.q: When does a penalty begin on an Ohio County property tax bill?
faqs.a: January 1 starts it, with 5 percent added through the end of that month. Payments from November 2 to December 31 cost only the face amount.

faqs.q: Can a house with an unpaid tax bill still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is paid from your sale proceeds, based on a quote from the sheriff before April 15 or the County Clerk once that date is past.

faqs.q: Whom do I call to question my Ohio County valuation?
faqs.a: The PVA, 270-298-4433. Values are outside the sheriff's authority.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax on an Ohio County sale?
faqs.a: The seller does, at 50 cents per $500 of the price on the deed, rounded up. The clerk collects it first.
